newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO says cannot guarantee no more suicide bombs.
newsitem.headline: PLO says cannot guarantee no more suicide bombs.

text.p: The Palestinian Authority was trying to prevent more suicide bombings against Israel but could give no guarantees, a Palestinian newspaper quoted a senior PLO intelligence officer as saying.
Israeli security officials said they were on high alert to avert attacks such as Friday's when an Islamic militant blew himself up at a Tel Aviv cafe killing three women and wounding about 50 people.
Al-Hayat Al-Jadida newspaper on Wednesday quoted Palestinian intelligence head Amin al-Hindi as saying that Israel's settlement policy had created an atmosphere that could lead to suicide bombings.

"The Israeli prime minister's insistence on building a new settlement on Jabal Abu Ghneim and by ignoring all international covenants and agreements with the Palestinian Authority, has created a fertile ground for suicide attacks," Hindi said.

Asked about the possiblity of a new attack, al-Hayat al-Jadida quoted Hindi as saying: "The crisis in the political situation will lead to a security crisis ... We cannot guarantee that no new suicide attacks will take place even though we continue to take all precautionary measures to prevent that."
Israel's police chief pointed to the breakdown in relations between the two security establishments as creating volatile conditions.
"In this state of relations when there is no cooperation these are good conditions for the terrorist organisations to act," Assaf Hefetz to Israel Radio.
Israel enraged Palestinians when it sent bulldozers to start work on building 6,500 homes for Jews on a hill in Arab East Jerusalem called Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa in Hebrew.
Palestinians want the eastern part of the city Israel captured from Jordan in 1967 as the capital of a future state. Israel wants to maintain control of all of Jerusalem.
The Tel Aviv blast was the first suicide attack since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was elected last May on a promise of bringing "peace with security."
A former head of Israel's Mossad intelligence agency admitted Israel's ability to prevent such attacks was limited too.
"We should be alert without panicking, do everything possible in terms of prevention and we have to do everything possible, to have good intelligence," Shabtai Shavit told Israel Radio.
"But intelligence about an individual suicide is perhaps the hardest of all intelligence assignments."
